- Measured on: Avoid a bad hire, which is visible and attributed, more than a missed hire, which is neither
- Measured on: Fill the gap without the ramp-up cost of someone who needs teaching
- Measured on: Keep the team's own delivery on track while running the loop
- Could do (medium): Write the requirement list from last quarter's work — The requirements as written belong to this actor, and the list is what the keyword filter and the recruiter's screen are both built from. Checking each line against what the team delivered last quarter separates what the job uses from what a previous strong candidate happened to have. A year count larger than the age of the technology is checkable before the posting goes up. Costs: A shorter list brings more applications into a funnel this actor's own team staffs, and it gives up the requirement page as the argument for a higher level and a wider band.
- Could do (low): Put the house preferences into the interview brief — This actor sets what each interviewer asks, and holds the requirements only they know about. A preference about architecture or about vertical experience that is not in the brief is still scored in the room, and the candidate cannot design against a criterion they were not given. Costs: A preference in writing is open to challenge from the panel and from the recruiter, and one that cannot be put into a sentence does not make it into the brief.
- Could do (medium): Cap the take-home and floor the review time — The exercise and who reviews it are both this actor's to set. Work built over hours and read in minutes is scored on whatever the reader happened to open, and the note that comes out of it describes the review rather than the submission. Capping the candidate's hours without a floor under the reviewer's minutes moves the asymmetry rather than closing it. Costs: A three-hour sample carries less to go on, so more of the decision falls to the panel, and twenty minutes from each of two reviewers comes out of a sprint the team is already behind on.
- Could do (medium): Agree the decision rule before the first conversation — Whether a split panel becomes a hire is this actor's decision, and a unanimity requirement settles it in advance: one dissent and three produce the same outcome. Writing the rule down before the loop starts, including who breaks a tie, keeps an even split from being written up as a finding about the candidate. Costs: Naming the tiebreaker means this actor signs a hire the panel did not agree on, and a hire that goes wrong is visible for a year and carries their name.
- Could do (high): Freeze the requirements once the loop opens — The requirements as written are this actor's; whether a requisition closes is not. Assessments taken against one description do not carry over to another, so a change of stack or scope that arrives mid-loop belongs in the next posting rather than in the scoring of work already done. Everyone already inside is then measured against the description they were given. Costs: The loop runs to the end against a profile the team has moved past, and the change the requirements needed waits for a search that starts again from the posting.
- Could do (medium): Fix the assessed level before the loop opens — The level a candidate is assessed at is this actor's to set, and it is set at the in-depth review whether or not it was written down first. Naming the level, and what evidence meets it, before the loop opens means experience above the band is measured against the requirements rather than against a forecast about how long someone stays. Costs: A level fixed in advance removes the move of recovering a strong candidate at the level below, and where the level was set wrong the search runs again from the posting.

### public-policy — Public policy and industry standards

Regulators, labour law, and the conventions the market copies from itself. Sets the outer bounds and moves on a timescale no individual process can wait for.

- Decides: What must be disclosed — pay transparency rules being the clearest current example
- Decides: What automated decision-making is permitted, and what must be explainable
- Decides: Which employment relationships are possible in which jurisdiction
- Cannot see: How a rule is implemented once it reaches a configuration screen
- Cannot see: Practices that are legal, ordinary, and still produce the effects catalogued here
- Measured on: Rules that are enforceable and measurable, which is a narrower set than rules that would help
- Measured on: Not disrupting labour markets faster than they can absorb the change
- Could do (medium): Extend disclosure from the band to the level — A disclosure rule that reaches the band leaves unstated the level the band attaches to, and the level decides where inside the band an offer lands. Requiring the posting to name the level being hired at, and the band for that level, closes the branch of the compensation bind that a band alone leaves open. Costs: A band is a number on a page and a level is a claim about an internal grid, so each complaint needs records the regulator has to ask for separately. It also fixes at publication a level that is currently settled after the panel.
- Could do (medium): Require postings to name where employment is possible — Which employment relationships are possible in which jurisdiction is settled before anyone applies, and it is one of the few facts here that this actor defines rather than regulates at a distance. Requiring the posting to list the jurisdictions the role can actually be contracted in moves that fact to publication day instead of the screening call. Costs: The rule binds a posting readable everywhere to contracts possible in a few places, and the body writing it reaches only its own territory — which one that is, this atlas does not state. The employer must publish an entity map it holds internally, and postings that read as open narrow visibly.
- Could do (medium): Require postings to be dated and withdrawn on closure — What a public posting is — an advertisement, or a statement that funded work exists — is a disclosure question, and that is the question this actor reaches. A rule that a posting carries its publication date and comes down when the search ends makes the difference between an open search and a talent pool observable from outside. Costs: Two dates are cheap to check, but the fact that decides a breach — whether the search had ended — sits in records only the employer holds, so every complaint starts with disclosure. The rule also reaches sourcing that is legal and ordinary, which widens the perimeter it has to defend.
- Could do (high): Require every automated rejection to name its rule — Where an application is ended by a threshold rather than by a reader, whether that decision must be explainable already sits inside this actor's bounds. Attaching the duty to the ending rather than to the message means a rule that closes an application — a missing term, an unmet threshold, an elapsed review window — produces a statement the applicant can check instead of nothing. Costs: The duty is written for an employer and performed by a setting on a configuration screen the rule's author never sees, so the text has to fix responsibility somewhere between the party that buys the system and the party that ships it. Each stated reason is also a statement that can be disputed, and at the volume of ended applications that is a caseload before it is a remedy.
- Could do (medium): Require continuity-based ranking features to be documented and justified — A feature that scores the length of a break sits inside the automated decision-making whose bounds this actor sets, and it is the input that closes the gap-penalty loop. Requiring any ranking input derived from employment continuity to be documented and justified makes its presence checkable, which a prohibition on its own does not. Costs: The rule can only be checked where the feature is named in a model card or a settings screen, so it rests on a documentation duty that lands on a supplier rather than on the employer being regulated. Naming one input leaves its proxies — recency of the last role, density of transitions — outside the text until they are named too.
- Could do (low): Publish a common schema for posting terms and outcomes — The market copies conventions from itself faster than it absorbs rules, and this actor writes conventions as well as rules. A published schema — band, level, stages, jurisdictions, and a decline that names its stage and its criterion — gives the disclosure duties a shape that can be filled in once and read by machine. Costs: A schema carries no obligation, so it is adopted where it is cheaper than what it replaces and nowhere else. The categories fixed in the first version become the ceiling on what is disclosed later, and the body that publishes it owns the revisions for as long as anyone uses it.

### recruiter — Recruiter

The function that moves people through the funnel. Holds the most information about the process and the least authority over its outcome.

- Decides: Which applications are read and in what order
- Decides: What is disclosed at the screen, and when
- Decides: The wording of the rejection
- Decides: Whether a candidate is told a search has stalled
- Cannot see: What the panel actually scored, beyond the recommendation
- Cannot see: Whether finance will approve the headcount this quarter
- Cannot see: What the hiring manager privately requires but has not written down
- Measured on: Move the pipeline; time-to-fill is measured, time-to-clarity is not
- Measured on: Protect the relationship with the hiring manager, who is the internal client
- Measured on: Avoid saying anything that could be quoted back as a commitment
- Could do (medium): State the band before asking for a number — The screen is where compensation first comes up, and the order of the two questions is the recruiter's to set. Saying the band that is on the requisition, before asking what the candidate expects, removes the asymmetry that both branches of the compensation bind run on. Where no band has been set, saying that is also an answer the candidate can act on. Costs: It spends the flexibility of hearing the candidate's figure first, and it puts a number into the conversation that can be quoted back later as a commitment.
- Could do (medium): Name the stage and the criterion that ended it — The wording of the rejection belongs to this seat, and the same message can carry the stage the process ended at, the criterion that was named to the recruiter, and what the process never reached. Where the panel returned a recommendation without a criterion, the message records that no criterion was given, rather than a template sentence standing in its place. What can be written is bounded by what the recruiter was handed. Costs: Each message is written rather than selected, against a clock measured as time-to-fill, and asking the panel for a criterion spends standing with the hiring manager, who is the internal client.
- Could do (medium): Tell everyone still inside when a search stops moving — Whether a candidate learns that a search has stalled is decided in this seat, and it can be decided from what is visible here: the date of the last scheduling activity on the requisition. The message states that date and no more, because whether the headcount returns this quarter is not visible from here. Silence at this point is read as a decision about the candidate. Costs: Candidates who are told make other plans, and the message puts in writing that the internal client's search has stopped, against a seat measured on time-to-fill and on that relationship.
- Could do (medium): Name every stage and its date at the screen — What the process contains, how many conversations it has and when the first decision is due are disclosed at the screen or nowhere, and that disclosure sits in this seat. A candidate holding the list can tell a delay from an ending. When a round is added or a date moves, the same channel carries that within days to everyone already inside. Costs: A stated date is a commitment held against interviewer calendars this seat does not control, so every slip becomes a message that has to be written.
- Could do (medium): Say whether an approved requisition sits behind the call — Outreach and the first conversation are where the recruiter states what the contact is for. Whether a requisition is open and approved, or whether this is a pool for headcount that does not exist yet, is a fact available at the moment of contact. Without it, the silence that follows such a conversation is read as a decision about the candidate. Costs: It costs replies: outreach that states there is no open requisition gives less reason to answer, and reply volume is what the sourcing side of the pipeline is counted in.
- Could do (high): Set the reading order in advance and in writing — Which applications are read and in what order is decided in this seat, and the order can be fixed before the week's queue exists: a stated share of screening capacity for inbound, order of arrival within each source, and no sort on how recently someone was last employed. The rule adds no screening capacity; it decides once where the capacity goes, instead of deciding it profile by profile against the length of the queue. Costs: Reading without that sort covers fewer profiles per hour, and outbound candidates the hiring manager has asked about wait behind inbound ones.

## Eras

### era.zero_rates_and_a_same_year_deduction — Zero rates and a same-year deduction

For over a decade money cost nothing to borrow and engineering payroll reduced taxable income in the year it was paid. Both facts were policy, both were durable, and together they made an empty seat more expensive than a wrong hire.

- Span: 2008–2019
- The money: From 16 December 2008 the US policy rate sat at its floor for seven years, and the euro-area deposit rate was cut to zero in July 2012 and below zero in June 2014. Under section 174 as it then stood, research and experimental expenditures could be deducted in the year they were paid rather than charged to capital account. Borrowing to fund growth was close to free, and payroll spent building product reduced taxable income immediately.
- What it did to hiring: Headcount was the standard use of raised capital. A salary was a current-year deduction and the return on a hire was measured in growth rather than in margin, so teams were sized to a funded plan and the plan came before the revenue. A listing route stayed open to companies without trailing profits throughout the period, which meant payroll could run ahead of earnings without closing off the exit.
- How you got in: Demand for people who could do the work ran ahead of supply, so employers hired for potential and trained afterwards. A beginner's salary carried the same immediate deduction as a senior's, which made junior seats cheap to fund against the cost of leaving a seat empty. Self-teaching, a short conversion course and a first job with training attached were ordinary routes in.
- What closed it: Not by a contraction. In March 2020 the same policy floor was reimposed and fund flows stepped up by a multiple, and hiring plans were sized to capital raised rather than to current revenue.
- 0.00–0.25% — US federal funds target range, held at its floor (16 Dec 2008 – 15 Dec 2015, EVD-007)
- 0.00% → −0.50% — ECB deposit facility rate, at or below zero (11 Jul 2012 – 26 Jul 2022, EVD-008)
- 100% — Research and development payroll deductible in the year it was paid (to tax year 2021, EVD-012)
- 15–43% a year — US technology listings profitable on trailing earnings (2011–2021, EVD-011)

### era.the_record_funding_years — The record funding years

Two years in which the policy floor returned and venture funding roughly doubled its previous record. Headcount plans were set against committed capital rather than against bookings, and the terms of entry were set on the candidate's side.

- Span: 2020–2021
- The money: The policy rate returned to 0.00–0.25% on 16 March 2020 and stayed there for two years. US venture-backed companies raised $329.6 billion in 2021 against a previous record of $166.6 billion in 2020, and global venture investment reached $671 billion. The listing window stayed open to companies without earnings: of 121 US technology listings in 2021, 21% were profitable on trailing twelve-month earnings.
- What it did to hiring: With several years of funding raised at once, headcount was planned against committed capital rather than against bookings, and roles were opened before the work that would fill them was specified. Time-to-fill became the operative constraint, so loops were shortened, offers raised and candidate pools widened across locations. Recruiting functions were themselves staffed to the expanded plan.
- How you got in: Employers competed for candidates, so entry terms were set on the candidate's side: compressed interview loops, offers made on shorter evidence, and pay set by competing bids. Entry-level and career-change intake ran at volume, because the alternative was leaving funded seats empty. Holding a current job was not a precondition, and changing employer was the ordinary way to raise pay.
- What closed it: Two dated changes. The target range left the floor on 17 March 2022, and for tax years beginning after 31 December 2021 any amount paid in connection with developing software had to be capitalised and amortised over five years — so a developer's salary stopped reducing taxable income in the year it was paid.
- $329.6B — US venture-backed companies raised (2021, against $166.6B in 2020, EVD-009)
- $671B — Global venture capital invested (2021, EVD-010)
- 0.00–0.25% — US policy rate, back at its floor (16 Mar 2020 – 16 Mar 2022, EVD-007)
- 21% of 121 — US technology listings profitable on trailing earnings (2021, EVD-011)

### era.rates_up_payroll_repriced — Rates up, payroll repriced

The policy rate reached its cycle peak, technology equities repriced, every stage of the private funding chain contracted at once, and software payroll became something to amortise rather than deduct. The correction ran through announced reductions rather than through attrition.

- Span: 2022–2023
- The money: The federal funds target range reached a cycle peak of 5.25–5.50% effective 27 July 2023 and was held there for about fourteen months, and the technology-weighted NASDAQ Composite fell 36.4% from its November 2021 close to its December 2022 low. Every stage of the private chain contracted together: US venture deal value fell from $348.0 billion in 2021 to $170.6 billion in 2023, exit value hit a decade low of $61.5 billion, and new fund commitments fell to a six-year low of $66.9 billion. From tax years beginning after 31 December 2021, software development costs were amortised over five years for domestic research and fifteen for foreign research instead of being deducted when paid.
- What it did to hiring: Payroll was now both harder to refinance and slower to deduct, so plans were cut to the capital already in hand. Reductions were announced rather than absorbed through attrition: a tracker of publicly reported technology layoffs records 165,269 employees in 2022 and 265,660 in 2023, its highest year. Open requisitions were closed and filled positions eliminated, and the recruiting capacity built for the previous era was itself reduced.
- How you got in: Hiring narrowed to the replacement of specific departures, which meant a posted role described work someone had recently been doing. The evidence employers would accept narrowed with it: recent experience in the same title, at similar scale, in the same stack. The routes that worked when employers hired for potential produced no offers, because the seats being filled were defined by an incumbent's job description rather than by a plan.
- What closed it: The financial conditions reversed without the reduction reversing. The target range came off its peak on 18 September 2024 and the immediate domestic deduction was restored by statute in July 2025, but the headcount removed during the correction was not restored — so the reduced level carried forward as the baseline rather than as a trough.
- 5.25–5.50% — Peak US federal funds target range (27 Jul 2023 – 18 Sep 2024, EVD-016)
- −36.4% — NASDAQ Composite, record close to cycle low (19 Nov 2021 – 28 Dec 2022, EVD-017)
- $348.0B → $170.6B — US venture deal value (2021 → 2023, EVD-018)
- $61.5B — US venture exit value, a decade low (2023, EVD-018)
- 5 years domestic, 15 foreign — Software payroll amortised rather than deducted (tax years from 2022, EVD-013)
- 165,269 → 265,660 — Tracked technology layoffs, not a census (2022 → 2023, EVD-023)

### era.a_fixed_number_of_seats — A fixed number of seats

The conditions that made hiring expensive were reversed; the number of positions was not. The contraction now runs through the hiring channel rather than the separation channel, which is why it is competition for a fixed and shrinking number of seats rather than a shortage of qualified people.

- Span: 2024–2026
- The money: The tax treatment that penalised payroll was undone: section 174A, added on 4 July 2025, allows domestic research expenditure to be deducted when paid for tax years beginning after 31 December 2024, balances capitalised under the 2022–2024 rules may be recovered in one year or over two, and smaller taxpayers may elect back to 2022. Policy rates came off their cycle peak in September 2024. The inputs that made hiring expensive were reversed. The number of positions was not.
- What it did to hiring: The contraction runs through the hiring channel, not the separation channel. Official gross hires in the US information sector fell from 1,270,000 in 2022 to 903,000 in 2025 — down 28.9% — while official layoffs and discharges in the same series were roughly flat at 451,000, 399,000, 395,000 and 447,000. Openings averaged 224,000 a month in 2022 and 121,000 in 2025, and stood at 90,000 in June 2026. Sector payrolls fell from 3,115,000 in November 2022 to 2,780,000 in July 2026.
- How you got in: Incumbents vacate few seats: the information-sector quits rate was 1.1% in June 2026 against 1.9% in June 2022, and the total-private hires rate 3.7% against 4.7%. Applications per open role rose from 116 in 2022 to 244 in 2025 across one platform's benchmark. Software postings ran 69.3% senior and 4.5% entry-level in the first quarter of 2026, and payroll records show employment of developers aged 22–25 down close to 20% from its late-2022 peak while employment at older ages in the same occupation did not fall. Entry now means succeeding a specific incumbent rather than being trained into a funded seat.
- 100% — Immediate deduction restored for domestic research (tax years from 2025, EVD-015)
- 1,270,000 → 903,000 — Gross hires, US information sector (2022 → 2025, EVD-022)
- 451,000 → 447,000 — Layoffs and discharges, US information sector — roughly flat (2022 → 2025, EVD-021)
- 224,000/mo → 90,000 — Job openings, US information sector (2022 average → Jun 2026, EVD-020)
- 3,115,000 → 2,780,000 — Information-sector payrolls (Nov 2022 → Jul 2026, EVD-019)
- 1.9% → 1.1% — Quits rate, US information sector (Jun 2022 → Jun 2026, EVD-026)
- 4.7% → 3.7% — Hires rate, total private (Jun 2022 → Jun 2026, EVD-025)
- 116 → 244 — Applications received per open role, one platform's benchmark (2022 → 2025, EVD-027)
- 69.3% senior, 4.5% entry — Software postings by level, one job board (Q1 2026, EVD-028)
- ≈ −20% — Employment of software developers aged 22–25 (late 2022 → Sep 2025, EVD-029)
- 149,023 — Announced technology job cuts, not a census (Jan–Jul 2026, EVD-024)

## Evidence

### EVD-001 — Hidden Workers: Untapped Talent (HBS / Accenture)

Survey of 8,000 workers and 2,250 executives in the US, UK and Germany on automated hiring. 88% of employers agree that qualified high-skill candidates are vetted out of the process by applicant tracking systems because they do not match the exact criteria of the job description; the report attributes a large "hidden worker" population to configurable ATS exclusion rules and knock-out filters.

- Fuller, J. B., Raman, M., Sage-Gavin, E., & Hines, K. (2021). Hidden Workers: Untapped Talent. Harvard Business School Project on Managing the Future of Work & Accenture.
- https://www.hbs.edu/managing-the-future-of-work/research/hidden-workers-untapped-talent

### EVD-002 — Too Good to Hire? Capability and Inferences about Commitment in Labor Markets

Four experiments with hiring managers show that candidates signalling more capability than the role requires are perceived as less committed to the organization and are penalized in hiring decisions — direct evidence for "overqualified" rejections and the seniority double bind.

- Galperin, R. V., Hahl, O., Sterling, A. D., & Guo, J. (2020). Administrative Science Quarterly, 65(2), 275–313.
- https://doi.org/10.1177/0001839219840022

### EVD-003 — Duration Dependence and Labor Market Conditions: Evidence from a Field Experiment

Field experiment sending roughly 12,000 fictitious résumés to about 3,000 postings in 100 US cities: the probability of an interview callback falls sharply with the length of the current unemployment spell (most of the decline within the first eight months) and the penalty is stronger in tighter labor markets — employers use gap length as a screening signal.

- Kroft, K., Lange, F., & Notowidigdo, M. J. (2013). The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 128(3), 1123–1167.
- https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjt015

### EVD-004 — Job Seekers Beware of Ghost Jobs (Clarify Capital survey of hiring managers)

Survey of 1,045 managers involved in hiring (fielded 31 Aug – 1 Sep 2022) on job postings kept live without active hiring: about half keep postings open because they are "always open to new people", 43% cite giving the impression that the company is growing or keeping existing employees motivated, one in three postings had been active for more than 30 days, and one in four respondents did not plan to fill the role for three months or longer.

- Clarify Capital (2022). Job Seekers Beware of Ghost Jobs. Survey of 1,045 hiring managers, 31 Aug – 1 Sep 2022.
- https://clarifycapital.com/job-seekers-beware-of-ghost-jobs-survey

### EVD-005 — Salary Transparency: Growth Slows, but Momentum Continues (Indeed Hiring Lab)

Tracks the share of US job postings on Indeed that disclose pay: 57.8% in September 2024, up from 52.2% a year earlier, with wide variation by occupation. Roughly four in ten postings still omit compensation — the structural precondition for compensation-band discrepancies surfacing only at late stages.

- Indeed Hiring Lab (2024, October 23). Salary Transparency: Growth Slows, but Momentum Continues.
- https://hiringlab.indeed.com/2024/10/23/salary-transparency-growth-slows-but-momentum-continues/

### EVD-006 — Employment Interview Reliability: New Meta-Analytic Estimates by Structure and Format

Meta-analysis of 125 inter-rater reliability coefficients (N = 32,428): reliability is substantially higher for panel interviews than for separate interviews by different interviewers (.74 vs .44) and rises with interview structure — quantifying how much interviewer variance, rather than candidate performance, drives divergent verdicts.

- Huffcutt, A. I., Culbertson, S. S., & Weyhrauch, W. S. (2013). International Journal of Selection and Assessment, 21(3), 264–276.
- https://doi.org/10.1111/ijsa.12036

### EVD-007 — Federal funds target range and effective rate (FRED)

The FOMC held the federal funds target range at 0.00–0.25% from 16 December 2008 to 15 December 2015 and again from 16 March 2020 to 16 March 2022. In every full month inside those two windows the effective federal funds rate stayed between 0.05% and 0.22%. Verified against the full daily DFEDTARU/DFEDTARL series (2,556 and 731 daily observations respectively, no other value in either window) and the monthly FEDFUNDS series.

- Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (US), Federal Funds Target Range — Upper Limit [DFEDTARU], Lower Limit [DFEDTARL] and Federal Funds Effective Rate [FEDFUNDS], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 27 August 2026.
- https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU

### EVD-008 — ECB deposit facility rate (FRED)

The ECB deposit facility rate was cut to 0.00% on 11 July 2012, turned negative at −0.10% on 11 June 2014, reached −0.50% on 18 September 2019 and returned to 0.00% on 27 July 2022. Every one of the 3,668 daily observations between 11 July 2012 and 26 July 2022 is at or below zero.

- European Central Bank, ECB Deposit Facility Rate for Euro Area [ECBDFR], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 27 August 2026.
- https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ECBDFR

### EVD-009 — PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q4 2021

US venture-backed companies raised $329.6 billion in 2021, against a previous record of $166.6 billion in 2020. The report states the figures verbatim; they are data-provider estimates and are revised in later vintages.

- PitchBook Data and National Venture Capital Association, Q4 2021 PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, 13 January 2022.
- https://nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/Q4_2021_PitchBook_NVCA_Venture_Monitor.pdf

### EVD-010 — KPMG Venture Pulse, Q4 2021

Global venture capital investment totalled $671 billion across 2021, the highest annual figure in the series, of which $171.4 billion was invested in Q4 2021 across 8,710 deals. Underlying data provided by PitchBook as of 31 December 2021.

- KPMG Private Enterprise, Venture Pulse Q4 2021: Global analysis of venture funding, 19 January 2022, p. 7.
- https://assets.kpmg.com/content/dam/kpmg/xx/pdf/2022/01/venture-pulse-q4-2021.pdf

### EVD-011 — Technology IPO profitability, 1980–2025 (Ritter)

Of 121 US technology listings in 2021, 21% were profitable on trailing- twelve-month earnings. The profitable share ranged from 15% to 43% in every year from 2011 to 2021, so a listing route remained open to companies without trailing profits throughout the period.

- Ritter, Jay R. (2026). Initial Public Offerings: Technology Stock IPOs, Table 4b — Technology and Life Science Company IPOs, 1980–2025. University of Florida.
- https://web.archive.org/web/20260731141233/https://site.warrington.ufl.edu/ritter/files/IPOs-Tech.pdf

### EVD-012 — 26 U.S.C. §174 as it stood before 2022

Under section 174(a)(1) as it stood before the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act took effect, a taxpayer could treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in connection with a trade or business as expenses not chargeable to capital account, deductible in the year paid or incurred. Payroll spent on building product reduced taxable income in the same year it was spent.

- 26 U.S.C. §174, United States Code, 2017 Edition. U.S. Government Publishing Office.
- https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2017-title26/html/USCODE-2017-title26-subtitleA-chap1-subchapB-partVI-sec174.htm

### EVD-013 — 26 U.S.C. §174 after the 2017 amendment

Section 13206(a) of Public Law 115-97 rewrote section 174 to deny any current deduction for specified research or experimental expenditures and to require them to be charged to capital account and amortised ratably over five years beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which they are paid or incurred, effective for amounts paid or incurred in tax years beginning after 31 December 2021. Subsection (c)(3) treats any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of software as such an expenditure, so roughly 10% of a developer's salary was deductible in the year it was paid.

- 26 U.S.C. §174, United States Code, 2023 Edition. U.S. Government Publishing Office. Amendment: Pub. L. 115-97 §13206(a).
- https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title26/html/USCODE-2023-title26-subtitleA-chap1-subchapB-partVI-sec174.htm

### EVD-014 — Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (IRS)

IRS guidance on the 2025 restoration: foreign research or experimental expenditures keep the 15-year amortisation period; balances capitalised under the 2022–2024 rules may be recovered in full in the first tax year beginning after 31 December 2024 or ratably over two years; and a taxpayer meeting the section 448(c) gross-receipts test — $31,000,000 average annual gross receipts over the three prior tax years for a year beginning in 2025 — may elect the new treatment retroactively to tax years beginning after 31 December 2021, by 6 July 2026.

- Internal Revenue Service, Rev. Proc. 2025-28, Internal Revenue Bulletin 2025-38, sections 2.02, 2.03(1), 2.06 and 3.02(1).
- https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-28.pdf

### EVD-015 — 26 U.S.C. §174A — domestic research expenditures

Section 70302(a) of Public Law 119-21, enacted 4 July 2025, added section 174A, which allows a deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year notwithstanding section 263, with an election to capitalise and amortise them over not less than 60 months instead. Effective for amounts paid or incurred in tax years beginning after 31 December 2024.

- 26 U.S.C. §174A, Domestic research or experimental expenditures. Added by Pub. L. 119-21 §70302(a), 4 July 2025.
- https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/174A

### EVD-016 — FOMC policy rate decisions (Open Market Operations)

The FOMC raised the federal funds target range to 5.25–5.50% effective 27 July 2023, the peak of the tightening cycle, and held it there until the 25 basis point reduction of 18 September 2024 — roughly fourteen months.

- Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (US), Open Market Operations, policy tools archive.
- https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm

### EVD-017 — NASDAQ Composite Index (FRED)

The NASDAQ Composite fell 36.4% from its record close of 16,057.44 on 19 November 2021 to its cycle low close of 10,213.29 on 28 December 2022.

- NASDAQ OMX Group, NASDAQ Composite Index [NASDAQCOM], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 27 August 2026.
- https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NASDAQCOM

### EVD-018 — PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q4 2023

Every stage of the US private funding chain contracted at once. Deal value fell from $348.0 billion in 2021 to $170.6 billion in 2023. Exit value reached a decade low of $61.5 billion across an estimated 1,129 events. New fund commitments fell to a six-year low of $66.9 billion across 474 funds, against $169.2 billion in 2021 and $172.8 billion in 2022.

- PitchBook Data and National Venture Capital Association, Q4 2023 PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, January 2024.
- https://nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Q4-2023-PitchBook-NVCA-Venture-Monitor.pdf

### EVD-019 — US information-sector employment (BLS CES)

US payroll employment in the information sector (NAICS 51 — software publishing, data processing and telecommunications, but not computer systems design) fell from a November 2022 peak of 3,115,000 to 2,780,000 in July 2026, a decline of 335,000 or 10.8%. An official establishment survey, not a layoff tracker.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics, series CES5000000001 (All employees, thousands, information, seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/CES5000000001

### EVD-020 — Job openings, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

Job openings in the US information sector averaged 224,000 a month in 2022 and 121,000 a month in 2025, and stood at 90,000 in June 2026, against an April 2022 peak of 274,000.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTS510000000000000JOL (Job openings, information, total US, seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTS510000000000000JOL

### EVD-021 — Layoffs and discharges, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

Official separations in the US information sector were 451,000 in 2022, 399,000 in 2023, 395,000 in 2024 and 447,000 in 2025 — roughly flat across the period, and without the year-to-year collapse reported by tracked-layoff counts over the same span.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTU510000000000000LDL (Layoffs and discharges, information, total US, not seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTU510000000000000LDL

### EVD-022 — Hires, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

Gross hires in the US information sector fell from 1,270,000 in 2022 to 903,000 in 2025, a decline of 367,000 or 28.9%. The measure counts hiring flows, not layoff announcements.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTU510000000000000HIL (Hires, information, total US, not seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTU510000000000000HIL

### EVD-023 — Tracked technology layoffs (Layoffs.fyi)

A privately maintained tracker that compiles publicly reported layoff events at technology and startup companies worldwide, revised as new reports arrive. It is not a statistical census. It records 165,269 employees in 2022, 265,660 in 2023, 152,922 in 2024, 122,606 in 2025 and 127,180 between 1 January and 24 August 2026.

- Layoffs.fyi — Tech and Startup Layoff Tracker, per-year pages, retrieved 27 August 2026.
- https://layoffs.fyi/2026-layoffs/

### EVD-024 — Announced job cuts, technology sector (Challenger, Gray & Christmas)

A count of announcements of planned job cuts by US-based employers rather than of completed separations; not an official statistic. It reports 133,988 technology-sector cuts announced in 2024, 154,445 in 2025 and 149,023 between January and July 2026 — 67% above the 89,251 announced in the same months of 2025.

- Challenger, Gray & Christmas, Job Cut Announcement Report, July 2026.
- https://www.challengergray.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Challenger-Report-July-2026.pdf

### EVD-025 — Hires rate, total private (BLS JOLTS)

The seasonally adjusted hires rate for total private employment was 3.7% in June 2026 (preliminary), a full percentage point below its June 2022 level of 4.7%: fewer positions per hundred jobs are being filled each month.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTS100000000000000HIR (Hires rate, total private, seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTS100000000000000HIR

### EVD-026 — Quits rate, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

The seasonally adjusted quits rate in the US information sector was 1.1% in June 2026 (preliminary), down from 1.9% in June 2022: fewer seats are being vacated by the people already in them.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTS510000000000000QUR (Quits rate, information, seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTS510000000000000QUR

### EVD-027 — Applications per opening (Greenhouse hiring benchmarks)

Applications received per open role across the reporting platform's customer base rose from 116 in 2022 to 244 in 2025, an increase of 111%. The stated dataset covers over 6,000 companies and over 640 million applications, so it measures one platform's customers rather than the labour market.

- Greenhouse, The Hire Standard: hiring benchmarks report, North America, March 2026.
- https://www.greenhouse.com/recruiting-benchmarks

### EVD-028 — Seniority mix of software postings (Indeed Hiring Lab)

Senior-level roles accounted for 69.3% of software development postings and entry-level roles for 4.5% in the first quarter of 2026, measured on one job board's postings rather than on all vacancies.

- Indeed Hiring Lab, The Labor Market Is Tilting Toward Seniority, 23 July 2026.
- https://hiringlab.indeed.com/2026/07/23/the-labor-market-is-tilting-toward-seniority/

### EVD-029 — Employment of young software developers (Stanford Digital Economy Lab)

In payroll records covering 3.5–5 million workers a month, employment of software developers aged 22–25 fell by close to 20% between its late-2022 peak and September 2025, while employment for older workers in the same occupation did not fall. This is the paper's raw descriptive series for one occupation; its headline regression result — a 16% relative decline for ages 22–25 in AI-exposed occupations, controlling for firm-level shocks — is a different figure and should not be conflated with it.

- Brynjolfsson, E., Chandar, B., & Chen, R. (2025). Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence. Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 13 November 2025.
- https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/app/uploads/2025/11/CanariesintheCoalMine_Nov25.pdf

### EVD-030 — Applications per opening on a national IT job board (DOU)

Platform-reported counts for a single national IT job board. In March 2026 the board carried 7,987 openings and recorded 131,000 applications from 22,800 candidates — an average of 26 applications per opening, and 132 per opening in front-end development. The first quarter of 2026 carried 22,900 openings, 23% more than the same quarter of 2025. These are one board's own counts for one country, not a market-wide measure, and the average conceals the spread: the ratio differs by a factor of five between specialisations on the same board in the same month.

- Конкуренція серед розробників росте. ІТ-ринок праці у І кварталі 2026. DOU, 2026.
- https://dou.ua/lenta/articles/it-job-market-1-quarter-2026/

### EVD-031 — Self-selected survey of IT job seekers in one national market (DOU)

A web survey run on a national IT community site in March–April 2026, covering 3,777 professionals in the country, 943 working abroad, and 363 looking for a first job in the field. Respondents were not sampled: they answered a questionnaire published on a site they already read, and the publication states no recruitment method, response rate or weighting. It describes who chose to answer, which is a different population from everyone searching.

- Більше пошуку, менше оптимізму: як змінився ІТ-ринок праці — результати опитування DOU, 2026.
- https://dou.ua/lenta/articles/job-market-2026-part-1/

### EVD-032 — Pre-adverse-action disclosure in employment background checks (15 U.S.C. §1681b(b)(3))

Under US federal law, an employer intending to take adverse action based in whole or in part on a consumer report for employment purposes must first give the candidate a copy of the report and a written description of their rights. A separate route applies where the candidate applied remotely: notice may instead follow within three business days of the action, naming the reporting agency, stating that the agency did not make the decision, and telling the candidate they may request a free copy and dispute its accuracy. The statute therefore already requires disclosure of the record, but only the first route places it before the decision is final, and neither fixes how long an offer stays open while a disputed field is reconciled.

- 15 U.S.C. §1681b(b)(3) — Fair Credit Reporting Act, conditions on use of consumer reports for employment purposes.
- https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681b

### EVD-033 — Corrected validity estimates reorder the selection methods, and work samples fall furthest

Sackett et al. (2022) showed that the range-restriction corrections long used in personnel-selection meta-analyses systematically overstated validity, and re-estimated it. This paper reproduces the full table. Against the prior figures, the corrected operational validities are: structured interviews .42 (was .51), job knowledge tests .40 (was .48), empirically keyed biodata .38 (was .35), work sample tests .33 (was .54), general mental ability .31 (was .51), unstructured interviews .19 (was .38). Two readings matter here. Structured interviews become the strongest single predictor, ahead of general mental ability. And work sample tests fall furthest of anything in the table — .21 — so the familiar claim that a sample of the work is the best available signal no longer holds, though .33 still places it above general mental ability. These are correlations with job performance once hired. Nothing here measures whether a scoring scheme is applied consistently, published in advance, or opened at all.

- Sackett, P. R., Zhang, C., Berry, C. M., & Lievens, F. (2023). Revisiting the design of selection systems in light of new findings regarding the validity of widely used predictors. Industrial and Organizational Psychology, 16(3). Reproducing the corrected estimates of Sackett, Zhang, Berry & Lievens (2022), Journal of Applied Psychology 107(11), 2040–2068.
- https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/A20984B138319E3D432E643978BF026D/S175494262300024Xa.pdf/revisiting_the_design_of_selection_systems_in_light_of_new_findings_regarding_the_validity_of_widely_used_predictors.pdf

### EVD-034 — Postings without a fillable requisition, measured on one ATS platform (Greenhouse)

A hiring platform reports that in any given quarter 18–22% of the roles posted through it are classified by the vendor as postings not attached to a search that can be filled, and pairs this with a survey of 2,500 workers in the US, UK and Germany in which 61% said they had heard nothing after an interview. The first figure is the vendor's own classification of its own customers' postings and is not independently auditable; the second is a self-reported recollection, not a matched record. Together they establish that a posting's existence does not imply a live requisition behind it — not any proportion for the market as a whole.

- Greenhouse 2024 State of Job Hunting report. Platform classification of ghost jobs and survey of 2,500 workers across the US, UK and Germany.
- https://www.greenhouse.com/blog/greenhouse-2024-state-of-job-hunting-report

### EVD-035 — Stated requirements set above what current jobholders hold (HBS, Dismissed by Degrees)

Across 26 million job postings, 67% of postings for production supervisor asked for a college degree while 16% of the people then doing that job held one — a gap of 51 percentage points between what the posting required and what the role demonstrably ran on. The study covers middle-skill occupations in the United States, not software roles, so it evidences the mechanism — a requirement list assembled from something other than the work being done — rather than any figure for technical hiring. The report also surveyed 600 business and HR leaders.

- Fuller, J. B., & Raman, M. (2017). Dismissed by Degrees: How degree inflation is undermining U.S. competitiveness and hurting America's middle class. Harvard Business School, Accenture and Grads of Life, October 2017.
- https://www.hbs.edu/news/releases/degree-inflation-us-competetiveness

### EVD-036 — Whether an application was assessed at all is defined in regulation (41 CFR 60-1.3)

US federal contracting regulation turns on whether an expression of interest was actually assessed. An individual counts as an "Internet Applicant" only where, among four criteria, "the contractor considers the individual for employment in a particular position" — defined as assessing the substantive information provided against the qualifications for that position. The rule then states the converse plainly: where there is a large number of expressions of interest, the contractor does *not* consider an individual by using "data management techniques that do not depend on assessment of qualifications, such as random sampling or absolute numerical limits, to reduce the number of expressions of interest to be considered". So an application closed without being read is a category the law already names and treats differently from a reviewed decline. The rule binds federal contractors in the United States, it governs who must be counted rather than what a candidate is told, and it does not require a contractor to record why any individual went unconsidered.

- 41 C.F.R. §60-1.3, definition of "Internet Applicant", paragraphs (1)-(3). Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs.
- https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-41/subtitle-B/chapter-60/part-60-1/subpart-A/section-60-1.3

### EVD-037 — A rejection issued without human involvement is regulated in the EU (GDPR Art. 22)

Under EU data protection law a person has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them. Recital 71 names the case directly: "automatic refusal of an online credit application or e-recruiting practices without any human intervention", and states the person should have "the right to obtain human intervention, to express his or her point of view, to obtain an explanation of the decision reached after such assessment and to challenge the decision". The distinction the regulation turns on is whether a human was involved at all — the same line the US applicant rules draw, reached from the opposite direction: one governs who must be counted, this one governs what the person may demand. It binds processing in the EU, it says nothing about decisions a human did make, and a rejection preceded by genuine human review falls outside it.

- Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 22 and Recital 71.
- https://gdpr-info.eu/art-22-gdpr/

### EVD-038 — Publishing the band before the interview becomes a duty in the EU (Directive 2023/970, Art. 5)

EU law requires employers to give applicants the initial pay or its range for the advertised position, set on objective and gender-neutral criteria, "in a manner such as to ensure an informed and transparent negotiation on pay, such as in a published job vacancy notice, prior to the job interview or otherwise", and to state the applicable collective agreement where there is one. It also forbids asking an applicant about their pay history in current or previous employment, and requires vacancy notices and job titles to be gender-neutral. The directive is being transposed into national law across Member States, and the reporting duties in Article 9 begin on 7 June 2027 for the largest employers. It fixes when a number must be disclosed, not that the number cannot move afterwards.

- Directive (EU) 2023/970 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023, Article 5 (Pay transparency prior to employment).
- https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/970/oj/eng

### EVD-039 — Openings that exist because a rule requires them (Ukraine, civil service competitions)

Ukrainian law requires a competition to fill a civil service post: "З метою добору осіб, здатних професійно виконувати посадові обов'язки, проводиться конкурс на зайняття посади державної служби". The requirement covers vacant posts, posts held during an absence, and category "А" posts whose term is expiring. Whole classes of publicly advertised openings therefore exist because a statute mandates the competition, not because an employer freely chose to search outside — so a public posting is not by itself evidence that the outcome is open. The law governs the Ukrainian civil service, not private technical hiring, and it says nothing about whether any particular competition has a favoured candidate; it establishes only that mandated-posting regimes exist and are ordinary.

- Закон України «Про державну службу» № 889-VIII, стаття 22 (Конкурс на зайняття посади державної служби).
- https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/laws/show/889-19

### EVD-040 — Probation period limits and dismissal standards (Ukraine, Labour Code art. 26–28)

Articles 26–28 of the Labour Code of Ukraine (Кодекс законів про працю України) establish statutory boundaries for probationary periods: probation may not exceed three months for standard employees (or six months in exceptional cases agreed with trade unions). If the probation period expires and the employee continues working, they are deemed to have passed probation, and subsequent dismissal is permitted only under standard general grounds. During probation, termination for failure to meet the role's requirements requires written justification with three days' notice.

- Кодекс законів про працю України, статті 26, 27, 28 (Випробування при прийнятті на роботу, строк випробування, наслідки результату випробування).
- https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/laws/show/322-08

### EVD-041 — Statutory notice and contractual probation parameters (UK, Employment Rights Act 1996)

The UK Employment Rights Act 1996 (c. 18) sets statutory minimum notice periods (Section 86) and governs contractual rights during initial employment. While probation periods in the UK are contractual rather than statutory, an employer may terminate an accepted unconditional employment contract before day one or during probation only by providing the agreed contractual or statutory notice pay, establishing that pre-start revocation represents an actionable contractual termination rather than costless cancellation.

- UK Employment Rights Act 1996, Section 86 (Rights of employer and employee to minimum notice).
- https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1996/18/section/86

### EVD-042 — Internal Candidacy and Public Competition Governance (5 U.S.C. § 2301 & UK Civil Service Management Code)

5 U.S.C. § 2301 (Merit system principles) and the UK Civil Service Management Code (Section 1.1 on fair and open competition) require transparent declaration of whether positions are open exclusively to internal promotion slates or contested in open public competition. Open competitions running parallel to pre-identified incumbent candidacies must state evaluation rules explicitly to prevent deceptive solicitation of external applicant labor.

- 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(1) ('Recruitment should be from qualified individuals from appropriate sources in an endeavor to achieve a work force from all segments of society, and selection and advancement should be determined solely on the basis of relative ability, knowledge, and skills, after fair and open competition which assures that all receive equal opportunity.').
- https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/5/2301

### EVD-043 — Structured Selection Procedures and Evaluator Preparation (29 C.F.R. § 1607.4 & EU AI Act Annex III)

The EEOC Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures (29 C.F.R. § 1607.4) and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Annex III(4)(a)) mandate structured assessment mechanisms and verified evaluator competency in employment screening. Rushed, unreviewed interview panels operating without dedicated preparation time increase inter-rater noise and introduce arbitrary disqualification factors inconsistent with job-related qualification metrics.

- EEOC Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, 29 C.F.R. § 1607.4 (Information on impact) & Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Annex III, Item 4(a) (High-risk AI systems in recruitment and selection).
- https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XIV/part-1607

### EVD-044 — Promissory Estoppel and Pre-Employment Good Faith (Restatement of Employment Law § 2.02)

Section 2.02 of the Restatement of Employment Law (American Law Institute, 2015) and prevailing common-law promissory estoppel doctrines establish actionable employer liability when an employer makes representations of an existing, funded position to induce a prospective employee to incur detrimental reliance (e.g. resigning from prior employment, incurring moving costs) while knowing the underlying headcount authorization or budgetary certification had not been secured or had lapsed.

- Restatement of Employment Law § 2.02 (Promise of Employment: Reliance and Revocation) (American Law Institute, 2015).
- https://www.ali.org/publications/show/employment-law/

### EVD-045 — Candidate Dossier Retention and Talent Pool Transparency (GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) & EDPB Guidelines 3/2019)

Article 5(1)(e) of the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) and European Data Protection Board Guidelines 3/2019 establish strict storage limitation principles for recruitment candidate data: holding candidate evaluation records in 'talent pool' pools beyond the initial hiring process requires explicit consent or legitimate interest bounded by stated expiration dates and transparent re-entry criteria.

- Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 5(1)(e) ('kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed').
- https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj

### EVD-046 — The Algorithmic Barrier: Quantifying Frictional Unemployment in Automated Recruitment (Fofanah, 2026)

Benchmarks a legacy keyword-based ATS parser against a proposed semantic matching system on the same applicant pool. The legacy system's recall is 0.45 (vs. 0.92 for the semantic system) — meaning most qualified candidates in the pool are never surfaced to a reviewer. The paper's error-mode analysis attributes over 40% of the legacy system's false negatives to pure lexical variation: a candidate's CV describing work in different wording from the posting's exact required terms (e.g. "client engagement" where the rubric expects "customer success"), not a genuine skills gap.

- Fofanah, I. D. (2026). The Algorithmic Barrier: Quantifying Artificial Frictional Unemployment and Information Asymmetry in Automated Recruitment Systems. arXiv:2601.14534.
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14534

### EVD-047 — Algorithmic Bias In Recruitment: Evaluating Resume Screeners & Video Analysis (Yadav & Ahirwar, 2026)

Reports that unaudited AI resume/video screeners produce a Disparate Impact Ratio below 0.72 for protected groups (improving to 0.88 once mitigation is applied), and documents proxy discrimination through indirect semantic associations with zip code, university tier, and employment-gap language. Caveat: published in the International Journal for Novel Research in Economics, Finance and Management, a venue not indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, or Google Scholar at the time this record was added — treat the underlying methodology as unverified even though the document itself states these figures verbatim.

- Yadav, K., & Ahirwar, K. (2026). Algorithmic Bias In Recruitment: Evaluating the Fairness and Diversity Impact of AI-Driven Resume Screeners and Video Interview Analysis. International Journal for Novel Research in Economics, Finance and Management.
- https://ijnrefm.com/algorithmic-bias-in-recruitment-evaluating-the-fairness-and-diversity-impact-of-ai-driven-resume-screeners-and-video-interview-analysis/

### EVD-048 — Behind the privilege shield: Safeguarding AI bias-testing data in employment decisions (Norton Rose Fulbright, 2026)

Legal analysis of a May 28, 2026 discovery order in Mobley v. Workday (N.D. Cal.), the pending federal case alleging that Workday's applicant screening tool produces disparate impact against candidates by age, race and disability. The order held that AI bias-testing analyses can be shielded by attorney-client privilege where outside counsel meaningfully directed the testing for legal-advice purposes — quoting the court's finding that "Workday has shown more than mere direction by its attorneys" — while the underlying raw factual data and any regulator-facing reports remain discoverable. Note: this record covers only the privilege ruling; Mobley v. Workday's substantive disparate-impact and "agent of the employer" theories remain contested litigation, not adjudicated fact — an earlier July 2024 order only denied a motion to dismiss those theories on plausibility grounds, and a nationwide ADEA collective was preliminarily certified in May 2025.

- Norton Rose Fulbright, Inside Tech Law (2026, June). Behind the privilege shield: Safeguarding AI bias-testing data in employment decisions.
- https://www.insidetechlaw.com/blog/2026/06/behind-the-privilege-shield-safeguarding-ai-bias-testing-data-in-employment-decisions
